params.system:
You are an independent expert referee assessing the SHARPNESS of mathematical results in a research project on the
asymptotic theory of a sequential Monte Carlo method for Bayesian variable selection (linear regression, p <= n^A, often
p >> n). Every result is asymptotic; finite-n behaviour is not a defect. The project's main risk is publishing theorems
that are correct but weaker than what is achievable.

You receive the working files of one ticket and a list of headline claims located by file and line span. Ignore any
status, score or review verdict the files assert. Take each claim as correct; your job is NOT to re-check the proof.

For each claim assess:
(a) hypotheses: is any assumption stronger than the proof needs (say which weaker condition suffices, with the step
    where it is used), or is it necessary (give a counterexample or a known lower bound showing that)?
(b) conclusion: is the rate, constant regime, scaling range (e.g. the exponent range for p vs n, beta-min level, sparsity
    growth) or mode of convergence improvable? Compare with the best known results for Bayesian variable selection
    (e.g. Johnson-Rossell, Narisetty-He, Castillo-Schmidt-Hieber-van der Vaart, Yang-Wainwright-Jordan MCMC mixing,
    Song-Liang, Zhou-Yang-Chang-Liang); cite only results you are confident about, and say when you are unsure.
(c) the cheapest concrete route to a stronger version, if one exists, and how hard it looks.

Severity: SHARP = no improvement you can justify; IMPROVABLE-EASY = a stronger version follows with a modest change you
can describe; IMPROVABLE-HARD = a stronger version is plausible or known elsewhere but needs new work; UNCLEAR = cannot
judge from the material.

Output, in this order:
1. For each claim, a short section: claim id, the assessment (a)-(c) with exact locations (file:line).
2. Then exactly one line per claim, nothing after the last one:
SHARP <claim id> VERDICT=<SHARP|IMPROVABLE-EASY|IMPROVABLE-HARD|UNCLEAR>

 145| independent one, E[g_n(κ_n, W_n) | 𝓕_n] = G_n(κ_n) a.s. By MIS-R (i), G_n(κ) ≤ C r_n for every κ ∈ 𝒦_n(s, A, M, φ₀, C_OS, c)
 146| and n ≥ n₀. Hence E[δ_n | 𝓕_n] ≤ C r_n a.s. on {κ_n ∈ 𝒦_n(…)} (an event of 𝓕_n: the class is a Borel subset of 𝔎_n,
 147| being defined on each stratum by finitely many inequalities between Borel functions — eigenvalues, determinants and
 148| ranks of Gram matrices, quadratic forms). For 𝒜_n ∈ 𝓕_n inside that event:
 149| E[δ_n 1_{𝒜_n}] = E[1_{𝒜_n}E[δ_n | 𝓕_n]] ≤ C r_n P(𝒜_n), and E δ_n ≤ E[δ_n 1_{𝒜_n}] + P(𝒜_nᶜ) (δ_n ≤ 1). By M.1 (2a)–(2c),
 150| {HPM ≠ S₀(κ_n)} ∪ {MPM ≠ S₀(κ_n)} ⊆ {δ_n ≥ ½} and {ξ_q ≠ S₀(κ_n)} ⊆ {δ_n ≥ min(q, 1 − q)}, so e.g.
 151| P(HPM ≠ S₀(κ_n)) ≤ P(𝒜_nᶜ) + P(δ_n ≥ ½, 𝒜_n) ≤ P(𝒜_nᶜ) + 2C r_n. The same argument with the functionals
 152| π_𝒞(S ⊋ S₀(κ)), π_𝒞(S ∌ j), π_𝒞(S ⊉ J^M_n(κ; c)), π_𝒞(Ω∖𝒩_n(κ; c)) in place of δ (each a Borel function of (κ, w); for the coordinate
 153| clause j is a fixed label and the event is {κ_n ∈ 𝒦⁰_n, j ∈ J^M_n(κ_n; c)}) gives the conditional versions of §3, and
 154| with 𝒦^λ_n that of the second sentence of §2. ∎
 155| 
 156| **(b)** On 𝒜_n ∩ {s(κ_n) = s′} (an event of 𝓕_n), κ_n ∈ 𝒦_n(s′, A, M, φ₀, C_OS, c) with c > c₁(s′, A), so by (a) for the
 157| slice s′, E[δ_n | 𝓕_n] ≤ C(s′) r_n a.s. there, for n ≥ n₀(s′). The finitely many slices s′ ∈ {1, …, s̄} cover 𝒜_n; take
 158| the maxima of n₀(s′) and C(s′). ∎
 159| 
 160| **(c)** Fix η > 0 and its constants, events 𝒜^η_n, and (n₀^η, C^η) from (b). For n ≥ n₀^η and L > 0, by Markov's
 161| inequality on 𝒜^η_n: P(δ_n > L r_n) ≤ P((𝒜^η_n)ᶜ) + E[δ_n 1_{𝒜^η_n}]/(L r_n) ≤ P((𝒜^η_n)ᶜ) + C^η/L. Hence
 162| limsup_n P(δ_n > L r_n) ≤ η + C^η/L, and lim_{L→∞} limsup_n P(δ_n > L r_n) ≤ η. As η is arbitrary the limit is 0:
 163| δ_n = O_P(r_n). By M.1 (1a) the same holds for max_j |PIP_j − 1{j ∈ S₀(κ_n)}| ≤ δ_n. Finally
 164| P(HPM ≠ S₀(κ_n)) ≤ P((𝒜^η_n)ᶜ) + 2C^η r_n, so limsup_n ≤ η for every η, i.e. → 0; likewise MPM. ∎
 165|

 167| independent of 𝓕_n. With 𝓕_n = σ(X^r_𝒞) and a regular conditional law this reads: given X^r_𝒞 = x,

asymptotic theory of a sequential Monte Carlo method for Bayesian variable selection (linear regression, p <= n^A, often

can describe; IMPROVABLE-HARD = a stronger version is plausible or known elsewhere but needs new work; UNCLEAR = cannot
judge from the material.

   1| # B — Corollary B: a sparsity obstruction on every design (W3-PSHARP, Claim B)
   2| 
   3| Status: **PROVED (by this seat, unchecked)**. Check record: see `../REPORT.md` §2.
   4| Notation: `../STATEMENT.md` §0, §3. Uses only Lemma S(1), (2) (`S_one_step.md`).
   5| 
   6| ## Statement
   7| For every n ≥ 3, every standardised design with p ≥ 2, every data set and every S₀ ⊆ [p] with 0 ≤ s₀ ≤ K − 1:
   8|   δ_n/(1 − δ_n) ≥ 𝒪^{lb}_n := Σ_{j=1}^{K−s₀} C(s₀+j, j) n^{−j/2} Π_{i=0}^{j−1} (p − s₀ − i)/(2p − 1 − s₀ − i) ≥ c(p, s₀)/√n,
   9| c(p, s) = (s+1)(p−s)/(2p−1−s); equivalently π(S₀) ≤ 1/(1 + 𝒪^{lb}_n), and in particular π(S₀) ≤ √n/(√n + c(p, s₀)). Moreover c(p, s₀) ≥ (s₀+1)/3 if s₀ ≤ p/2;
  10| c(p, s₀) ≥ 1 if s₀ ≥ 1; c(p, 0) > ½; c(p, s₀)/(s₀+1) → ½ if p → ∞ and s₀/p → 0.
  11| 
  12| ## Proof
  13| Fix 1 ≤ j ≤ K − s₀ and J ⊆ [p]∖S₀ with |J| = j; S_J := S₀ ∪ J ∈ Ω and (normalising constant cancelled)
  14|   π(S_J)/π(S₀) = [w(s₀+j)/w(s₀)] · (D_{S₀}/D_{S_J})^{1/2} · ((2b₀ + Q_{S₀})/(2b₀ + Q_{S_J}))^{ν}.
  15| Adding the columns of J one at a time, Lemma S(2) gives Q_{S_J} ≤ Q_{S₀}, so the last factor is ≥ 1, and Lemma S(1)
  16| gives D_{S_J}/D_{S₀} ≤ n^{j}. (Lemma S is applied to intermediate sets of size ≤ s₀ + j − 1 ≤ K − 1.) Hence
  17| π(S_J)/π(S₀) ≥ [w(s₀+j)/w(s₀)] n^{−j/2}. There are C(p − s₀, j) such J (j ≤ K − s₀ ≤ p − s₀); the models S_J are
  18| distinct and different from S₀; so
  19|   δ_n/(1 − δ_n) = Σ_{S≠S₀} π(S)/π(S₀) ≥ Σ_{j=1}^{K−s₀} C(p − s₀, j) [w(s₀+j)/w(s₀)] n^{−j/2}.
  20| Prior: w(s₀+j)/w(s₀) = C(2p−1, s₀)/C(2p−1, s₀+j) = [(s₀+j)!/s₀!] / Π_{i=0}^{j−1}(2p−1−s₀−i), and
  21| C(p−s₀, j) = Π_{i=0}^{j−1}(p−s₀−i)/j!. Their product is C(s₀+j, j) Π_{i=0}^{j−1}(p−s₀−i)/(2p−1−s₀−i): this is 𝒪^{lb}_n.
  22| All terms are positive and the j = 1 term is (s₀+1)(p−s₀)/((2p−1−s₀)√n) = c(p, s₀)/√n. Since π(S₀) = 1/(1 + δ_n/(1−δ_n)),
  23| π(S₀) ≤ 1/(1 + 𝒪^{lb}_n) ≤ 1/(1 + c/√n).
  24| 
  25| Constants. (i) s₀ ≤ p/2: (p−s₀)/(2p−1−s₀) ≥ 1/3 ⟺ 3p − 3s₀ ≥ 2p − 1 − s₀ ⟺ p + 1 ≥ 2s₀. (ii) s₀ ≥ 1:
  26| c ≥ 1 ⟺ (s₀+1)(p−s₀) ≥ 2p−1−s₀ ⟺ (s₀−1)(p−s₀−1) ≥ 0, true since p ≥ s₀ + 1. (iii) c(p, 0) = p/(2p−1) > ½.
  27| (iv) c/(s₀+1) = (1 − s₀/p)/(2 − (1+s₀)/p) → ½ when p → ∞ and s₀/p → 0. ∎
  28| 
  29| ## Consequences (sequences with s₀ ≤ min(K − 1, p/2); any designs; any data)
  30| Put a_n := (s₀+1)/(3√n), deterministic. By the above, **for every data set**, δ_n/(1−δ_n) ≥ a_n, i.e.
  31| π(S₀) ≤ 1/(1 + a_n) and δ_n ≥ a_n/(1 + a_n).
  32| - **B1.** If π(S₀) → 1 in probability along a subsequence, then 1/(1 + a_n) → 1 along it (a deterministic upper bound of
  33|   a sequence converging to 1 in probability), so s₀ = o(√n) there. If s₀ ≥ λ√n: a_n ≥ λ/3 and π(S₀) ≤ 1/(1 + λ/3). If
  34|   s₀/√n → ∞: π(S₀) ≤ 1/(1 + a_n) → 0, surely.
  35| - **B1, critical scale.** Let s₀/√n → λ ∈ (0, ∞) and s₀/p → 0 (so s₀ → ∞, p → ∞, and K − s₀ → ∞ because
  36|   s₀ = o(n) and p − s₀ → ∞). Fix j ≥ 1. For n large, j ≤ K − s₀, and the j-th term of 𝒪^{lb}_n is
  37|   C(s₀+j, j) n^{−j/2} Π_{i<j}(p−s₀−i)/(2p−1−s₀−i) → (λ^j/j!)·2^{−j}: C(s₀+j, j) n^{−j/2} = Π_{l=1}^{j}((s₀+l)/√n)/j! → λ^j/j!, and each
  38|   of the j factors (p−s₀−i)/(2p−1−s₀−i) = (1 − (s₀+i)/p)/(2 − (1+s₀+i)/p) → ½. All terms are ≥ 0, so for every J:
  39|   liminf 𝒪^{lb}_n ≥ Σ_{j=1}^{J}(λ/2)^j/j!; letting J → ∞, liminf 𝒪^{lb}_n ≥ e^{λ/2} − 1, and
  40|   limsup π(S₀) ≤ limsup 1/(1 + 𝒪^{lb}_n) ≤ e^{−λ/2}, for every sequence of designs and data sets.
  41| - **B2.** Let ρ_n → 0 be deterministic and δ_n = O_P(ρ_n): there is C with P(δ_n ≤ Cρ_n) ≥ ½ for all large n. On that
  42|   (nonempty) event a_n/(1 + a_n) ≤ δ_n ≤ Cρ_n; a_n is deterministic, so a_n/(1+a_n) ≤ Cρ_n for all large n, hence
  43|   a_n ≤ 2Cρ_n eventually: s₀ + 1 = O(√n ρ_n). With ρ_n = r_n: s₀ = O(√(log n)). The claim "s₀ = O(1) on the witness
  44|   sequences of Corollary A2 with log p ≍ log n" is proved in `A_log_factor.md` §6.
  45| - **B3** is a reading of B1, B2 and Corollary A2 (no further mathematical content): on the witness sequences of
  46|   Corollary A2 with log p ≍ log n the rate r_n cannot hold with s₀ → ∞; there any concentration theorem must allow the
  47|   rate (s₀+1)√(log p/n), and π(S₀) → 1 needs s₀ = o(√(n/log p)); on every design, π(S₀) → 1 needs s₀ = o(√n).
  48| 
  49| ## Remarks
  50| 1. **Relation to the parents (not used above).** The first display is `W3-POST2:A2` (δ_n ≥ 𝒪⁰_n/(1 + 𝒪⁰_n)) with
  51|    D_{S_J}/D_{S₀} ≤ n^{|J|} inserted, i.e. 𝒪⁰_n ≥ 𝒪^{lb}_n. Its j = 1 term with c(p, s₀) ≥ 1 is [LB] with n in place of
  52|    n + 1, on [LB]'s domain (1 ≤ s₀ < p, s₀ + 1 ≤ K), without s₀ ≤ p/2; s₀ = 0 is added (constant > ½).
  53| 2. **Equality.** If X is orthogonal and y ⟂ col X, every D ratio is n and every fit factor is 1, so the superset odds
  54|    equal 𝒪^{lb}_n exactly (`../numerics/b_check_out.txt`, F2, "equality case": 1.000000000000).
  55| 3. **Size of the full sum.** Table T1 of `b_check_out.txt` agrees with the critical-scale limit of B1 (e.g. λ = 4,
  56|    p = 10n: 1/(1 + 𝒪^{lb}_n) = 0.1353 at n = 10⁶, e^{−2} = 0.1353, against the j = 1 cap 0.3333).
  57| 4. **Falsification.** `../numerics/b_check.py` F2: 55,740 triples (design, data, S₀) — every S₀ with s₀ ≤ K − 1, not
  58|    only a true support; iid, equicorrelated, duplicated, near-duplicated, orthogonal and binary designs; null, sparse,
  59|    dense, near-exact and Cauchy responses; n from 6 to 5000 — minimum of odds/𝒪^{lb}_n = 1.033.

   1| # S — one-step supersets with the fit factor kept (W3-PSHARP, Lemma S and Lemma V)
   2| 
   3| Status: **PROVED (by this seat, unchecked)**. Check record: see `../REPORT.md` §2.
   4| Notation: `../STATEMENT.md` §0 (the coded target π of [W3P] §0). Self-contained: nothing is cited beyond the
   5| definition of π.
   6| 
   7| ## Lemma V (variational form of Q; scaling)
   8| For every S ⊆ [p] (any size, S = ∅ included) and every standardised y:
   9|   Q_S = min_{ϑ∈ℝ^S} { ‖y − X_Sϑ‖² + ϑᵀ(G_S + I)ϑ/n } ≥ 0,
  10| and, with Cy^r = s_y y,
  11|   s_y² Q_S = min_{ϑ∈ℝ^S} { ‖Cy^r − X_Sϑ‖² + ϑᵀ(G_S + I)ϑ/n }.
  12| *Proof.* ‖y − X_Sϑ‖² + ϑᵀ(G_S + I)ϑ/n = yᵀy − 2z_Sᵀϑ + ϑᵀ[G_S + (G_S + I)/n]ϑ = yᵀy − 2z_Sᵀϑ + ϑᵀH_Sϑ/n, because
  13| G_S + (G_S + I)/n = ((n + 1)G_S + I)/n = H_S/n. H_S is positive definite, so the minimum is at ϑ = nH_S⁻¹z_S, with
  14| value yᵀy − n z_SᵀH_S⁻¹z_S = Q_S. The objective is a sum of two nonnegative terms, so Q_S ≥ 0. The second display is
  15| the first multiplied by s_y², with ϑ replaced by ϑ/s_y. (S = ∅: Q_∅ = yᵀy.) ∎
  16| 
  17| ## Lemma S
  18| Let n ≥ 3, X a standardised design with p ≥ 2, y a standardised response, S ⊆ [p] with |S| + 1 ≤ K, j ∉ S. Write
  19| G := G_S, H := H_S, A := G + I, g := g_{S,j} = X_Sᵀx_j, s := s_{S,j} = n² − (n + 1)²gᵀH⁻¹g, S⁺ := S ∪ {j}.
  20| (If S = ∅: g is void, s = n², and every quadratic form in g is 0.)
  21| 
  22| **1. Determinant.** D_{S⁺}/D_S = s/(n − gᵀA⁻¹g); 0 < s ≤ n²; D_{S⁺}/D_S ≤ n, with equality iff x_j ⟂ col X_S; and
  23| D_{S∪J}/D_S ≤ n^{|J|} for every J disjoint from S.
  24| 
  25| *Proof.* Order the columns as (X_S, x_j). Since ‖x_j‖² = n − 1,
  26|   H_{S⁺} = [[H, (n+1)g], [(n+1)gᵀ, (n+1)(n−1) + 1]] = [[H, (n+1)g], [(n+1)gᵀ, n²]],  G_{S⁺} + I = [[A, g], [gᵀ, n]].
  27| Both matrices are positive definite (G_{S⁺} ⪰ 0), and so are H and A. By the Schur complement formula,
  28| det H_{S⁺} = det H · (n² − (n+1)²gᵀH⁻¹g) = det H · s and det(G_{S⁺} + I) = det A · (n − gᵀA⁻¹g), and both Schur
  29| complements are positive. Hence D_{S⁺}/D_S = s/(n − gᵀA⁻¹g), and 0 < s ≤ n² (H⁻¹ ⪰ 0).
  30| The inequality s ≤ n(n − gᵀA⁻¹g) is equivalent to gᵀ[(n+1)²H⁻¹ − nA⁻¹]g ≥ 0. H and A are functions of G, hence
  31| simultaneously diagonalisable; on an eigenvector of G with eigenvalue λ ≥ 0 the matrix (n+1)²H⁻¹ − nA⁻¹ has eigenvalue
  32|   (n+1)²/((n+1)λ + 1) − n/(λ + 1) = [(n+1)λ + n² + n + 1] / [((n+1)λ + 1)(λ + 1)] > 0
  33| (numerator: (n+1)²(λ+1) − n((n+1)λ + 1) = (n+1)λ + (n+1)² − n). So it is positive definite: the inequality holds,
  34| with equality iff g = 0, i.e. x_j ⟂ col X_S. The last claim follows by adding the columns of J one at a time: the
  35| matrices H_·, G_· + I and the identity above are defined for every subset of [p], whatever its size. ∎
  36| 
  37| **2. Fit.** With ρ̃_S := y − (n+1)X_SH⁻¹X_Sᵀy:  Q_S − Q_{S⁺} = n (x_jᵀρ̃_S)²/s ≥ (x_jᵀρ̃_S)²/n ≥ 0, and 0 ≤ Q_{S⁺} ≤ Q_S.
  38| 
  39| *Proof.* For a positive definite block matrix M = [[H, h], [hᵀ, d]] and v = (v₁, v₂),
  40| vᵀM⁻¹v = v₁ᵀH⁻¹v₁ + (v₂ − hᵀH⁻¹v₁)²/(d − hᵀH⁻¹h) (block inversion). With M = H_{S⁺}, h = (n+1)g, d = n², v = (z_S, z_j),
  41| z_j = x_jᵀy: v₂ − hᵀH⁻¹v₁ = x_jᵀy − (n+1)x_jᵀX_SH⁻¹X_Sᵀy = x_jᵀρ̃_S and d − hᵀH⁻¹h = s. Therefore
  42| z_{S⁺}ᵀH_{S⁺}⁻¹z_{S⁺} − z_SᵀH⁻¹z_S = (x_jᵀρ̃_S)²/s, and Q_S − Q_{S⁺} = n(x_jᵀρ̃_S)²/s. The lower bound uses s ≤ n². Q_{S⁺} ≥ 0
  43| by Lemma V. ∎
  44| 
  45| **3. One model.** Let S = S₀ (so s₀ + 1 ≤ K) and γ_j := (Q_{S₀} − Q_{S₀∪{j}})/(2b₀ + Q_{S₀}). Then γ_j ∈ [0, 1) and
  46|   π(S₀∪{j})/π(S₀) ≥ [(s₀+1)/(2p−1−s₀)] n^{−1/2} (1 − γ_j)^{−ν} ≥ [(s₀+1)/(2p−1−s₀)] n^{−1/2} e^{νγ_j}.
  47| 
  48| *Proof.* Both models are in Ω, and the normalising constant of π cancels:
  49|   π(S₀∪{j})/π(S₀) = [w(s₀+1)/w(s₀)] · (D_{S₀}/D_{S₀∪{j}})^{1/2} · ((2b₀ + Q_{S₀})/(2b₀ + Q_{S₀∪{j}}))^{ν}.
  50| Prior: w(s₀+1)/w(s₀) = C(2p−1, s₀)/C(2p−1, s₀+1) = (s₀+1)/(2p−1−s₀). Determinant: ≥ n^{−1/2} by item 1.
  51| Fit: (2b₀ + Q_{S₀∪{j}})/(2b₀ + Q_{S₀}) = 1 − γ_j, and 0 ≤ Q_{S₀∪{j}} ≤ Q_{S₀} with b₀ > 0 give 0 ≤ γ_j < 1. Finally
  52| −log(1 − γ) ≥ γ on [0, 1). ∎
  53| 
  54| **4. Sum.** For every 𝒩 ⊆ [p]∖S₀:  δ_n/(1 − δ_n) ≥ [(s₀+1)/(2p−1−s₀)] n^{−1/2} Σ_{j∈𝒩} e^{νγ_j}.
  55| 
  56| *Proof.* π(S₀) > 0 (every score is positive and finite), and δ_n/(1 − δ_n) = Σ_{S∈Ω, S≠S₀} π(S)/π(S₀). The models
  57| S₀∪{j}, j ∈ 𝒩, are distinct elements of Ω∖{S₀}; all other terms are ≥ 0. Apply item 3. ∎
  58| 
  59| ## Remarks
  60| 1. Item 1 improves the bound D_{S⁺}/D_S ≤ n + 1 used in [LB] line 25 to n, which is attained (orthogonal column).
  61| 2. Falsification: `../numerics/b_check.py` F1 → `b_check_out.txt` (8,064 pairs (S, j) on iid, correlated,
  62|    rank-deficient, near-duplicate, orthogonal and binary designs: both identities to 1e-12; max (D_{S⁺}/D_S)/n =
  63|    1.000000000000).

You are an independent expert referee assessing the SHARPNESS of mathematical results in a research project on the
asymptotic theory of a sequential Monte Carlo method for Bayesian variable selection (linear regression, p <= n^A, often
p >> n). Every result is asymptotic; finite-n behaviour is not a defect. The project's main risk is publishing theorems
that are correct but weaker than what is achievable.

You receive the working files of one ticket and a list of headline claims located by file and line span. Ignore any
status, score or review verdict the files assert. Take each claim as correct; your job is NOT to re-check the proof.

For each claim assess:
(a) hypotheses: is any assumption stronger than the proof needs (say which weaker condition suffices, with the step
    where it is used), or is it necessary (give a counterexample or a known lower bound showing that)?
(b) conclusion: is the rate, constant regime, scaling range (e.g. the exponent range for p vs n, beta-min level, sparsity
    growth) or mode of convergence improvable? Compare with the best known results for Bayesian variable selection
    (e.g. Johnson-Rossell, Narisetty-He, Castillo-Schmidt-Hieber-van der Vaart, Yang-Wainwright-Jordan MCMC mixing,
    Song-Liang, Zhou-Yang-Chang-Liang); cite only results you are confident about, and say when you are unsure.
(c) the cheapest concrete route to a stronger version, if one exists, and how hard it looks.

Severity: SHARP = no improvement you can justify; IMPROVABLE-EASY = a stronger version follows with a modest change you
can describe; IMPROVABLE-HARD = a stronger version is plausible or known elsewhere but needs new work; UNCLEAR = cannot
judge from the material.

Output, in this order:
1. For each claim, a short section: claim id, the assessment (a)-(c) with exact locations (file:line).
2. Then exactly one line per claim, nothing after the last one:
SHARP <claim id> VERDICT=<SHARP|IMPROVABLE-EASY|IMPROVABLE-HARD|UNCLEAR>

 293|   The global floor gives the anchored SE_lambda(j0) for the exact
 294|   j0=ceil((2A+1)s0)+1 and every larger set as well. It gives SE_w(m_sharp;g0)
 295|   for any fixed g0>0 once (n-1)c>=g0, irrespective of m_sharp. Finally
 296|   theta_lo^2 nc/(sigma^2 log n)->infinity proves BM-infinity.
 297| * (FL-16),(FL-Q): all principal Grams have floor c.
 298| * (V): in the G-inner product, for every |U|<=15 excluding j,
 299|   |Cov_G(j,signal|U)| >= |theta_j| c
 300|      - K_15 sum_{k!=j}|theta_k|(1+|j-k|)^(-alpha)
 301|      >= c theta_lo/2.
 302|   Terms indexed by k in U vanish. Since Var_G(j|U)<=1,
 303|   delta_{U,j}^2>=(n-1)c^2 theta_lo^2/4. Take
 304|   M_n=(n-1)c^2 theta_lo^2/(4 log n)->infinity.
 305| * (L-size^b),(L-feas): the proof of (2.1) and E2's feasibility argument
 306|   apply verbatim. Enlargement does not damage any other hypothesis.
 307| * (L-gain): for l outside Q, BC and Var_G(l|U)>=c give
 308| 
 309|       delta_{U,l}^2 <= (n-1) B_theta^2 K_15^2
 310|                              (1+R_Q)^(-2alpha)/c
 311|                      <= (B_theta^2 K_15^2/c) sqrt(log n).
 312| 
 313|   Since tau_U^2>=sigma^2, this is <=eta tau_U^2 log n eventually. For example
 314|   it suffices that sqrt(log n)>=B_theta^2 K_15^2/(c eta sigma^2).
 315|   Thus a fixed, arbitrarily small positive eta works; exact eta=0 is not
 316|   asserted for a nonzero decay tail. Alternatively, radius
 317|   ceil(D(n/log n)^gamma) gives leak level <=B_theta^2 K_15^2/(c sigma^2 D^(2alpha));
 318|   choose D to make this <=eta and take b>gamma to absorb its size constants.
 319| * (BM-W): theta_lo^2 nc/[sigma^2(q+log n)]->infinity, since q<=n^b, b<1.
 320|   This proves BM-Q, hence BM-W by RM2 `lemmas/L2_width.md:187-192`.
 321| * (W) through (W-loc): apply (0.1)-(0.2) to G. Use the same N_l and r as
 322|   in §0, any fixed h in (0,1/2-b), L_n=(1+JD)F(r)->0, and
 323|   eta_n=L_n^2/c. These meet the exact two inequalities and entropy/atom
 324|   budgets in RM2 §3.1, so (W-loc) implies (W) by RM2
 325|   `lemmas/L2_width.md:123-180`.
 326| 
 327| Every hypothesis of (C1) is now verified. The cutoff furnished by these
 328| lemmas is alpha>2, again because of IR, not because of a leak-size obstruction.
 329| 
 330| ## E4. One truth and polynomially many weak proxies
 331| 
 332| Status: PROVED (by this seat, unchecked).
 333| 
 334| Fix 0<b<1/2, C0>0 finite, sigma^2>0 and theta=theta_1!=0 fixed. Let
 335| p=floor(n/3), q=floor(n^b), r^2=C0 log n/n, and take centred orthonormal
 336| e_1,...,e_p. For sufficiently large n, 0<r<1 and q<=p. Use exactly
 337| 
 338|     z_1=e_1,
 339|     z_j=r e_1+sqrt(1-r^2)e_j  (2<=j<=q),
 340|     z_j=e_j                  (j>q),
 341|     x_j=sqrt(n-1) z_j,  Q={1,...,q}, S0={1}.
 342| 
 343| The proxy-proxy correlations are r^2, not zero. With m=q-1 the Gram on Q is
 344| 
 345|     G_Q = [1, r 1_m'; r 1_m, (1-r^2) I_m+r^2 1_m1_m'].
 346| 
 347| Its distance from identity in operator norm is at most
 348| 
 349|     epsilon_n=|r|sqrt(m)+r^2(m+1) ->0.
 350| 
 351| The other columns are an orthogonal identity block. Hence the full Gram has
 352| floor >=1/2 eventually; this proves (FL-16) and (FL-Q) with phi0^2=1/2.
 353| The same global floor verifies every anchored and weak SE in T1-F with,
 354| for example, A=1, g0=1; M=theta^2+1 bounds energy. BM-infinity follows from
 355| fixed |theta|>0. These are exactly all H0 clauses (GROW `STATEMENT.md:84-88`).
 356| There is no asymptotic lower threshold on |theta| and no upper or lower
 357| threshold on the fixed positive C0 beyond finiteness and positivity.
 358| 
 359| For any U excluding 1, the other outside-Q columns are orthogonal and at
 360| most 15 proxies can be in U. With t such proxies, direct Schur complementation
 361| of their equicorrelated Gram gives
 362| 
 363|     Var_G(1|U)=(1-r^2)/(1+(t-1)r^2),
 364| 
 365| with value 1 at t=0. It is >=1/2 eventually (also follows from the global
 366| floor). Thus delta_{U,1}^2=theta^2(n-1)Var_G(1|U)
 367| >=theta^2(n-1)/2; take M_n=theta^2(n-1)/(2 log n) for (V).
 368| 
 369| (L-size^b) holds exactly by q=floor(n^b); K=p and p>=2q+33 eventually,
 370| proving (L-feas). For every l>q, x_l is orthogonal to the whole remaining
 371| Gram, so its projection on every U excluding l is zero and
 372| u_{U,l}'mu=0: (L-gain) has eta=0, and b<beta(0,1)=1/2.
 373| BM-Q holds since theta^2 n/[2sigma^2(q+log n)]->infinity, hence BM-W.
 374| 
 375| Finally verify the exact definition of (W-loc). Put N_l={1} for 2<=l<=q,
 376| and N_l=empty for l=1 or l>q. Every lattice T contains 1. For a proxy
 377| l outside T, z_l-r z_1=sqrt(1-r^2)e_l is orthogonal to all of X_T,
 378| including the other proxies. Therefore beta_{T,l} has coefficient r at 1
 379| and zero elsewhere, exactly the regression on T intersect N_l={1}.
 380| For l>q both regressions are zero. There are no lattice pairs with l=1.
 381| Thus both (W-loc) inequalities hold with L_n=eta_n=0 and nu_n=1.
 382| Choose any h in (0,1/2-b); nu_n log 2<=h log n eventually. This proves (W),
 383| and hence verifies every (C1) hypothesis at genuine polynomial |Q|.
 384| 
 385| ## E5. A positive equicorrelation group: direct width verification
 386| 
 387| Status: PROVED (by this seat, unchecked), for the explicit range below.
 388| The larger candidate range is not asserted.
 389| 
 390| Fix 0<b<3/10, 0<a<1, theta!=0, sigma^2>0, all constant. Let
 391| p=floor(n/3), q=floor(n^b), Q={1,...,q}, S0={1}. Choose centred orthonormal
 392| e_0,e_1,...,e_p (p+1<=n-1 eventually), and set
 393| 
 394|     z_j=sqrt(a)e_0+sqrt(1-a)e_j  (j<=q),
 395|     z_j=e_j                    (j>q),
 396|     X=sqrt(n-1)[z_1 ... z_p], mu=theta x_1.
 397| 
 398| Thus the group has off-diagonal correlation a; the remainder is an independent
 399| orthogonal block. Every principal Gram has floor c=1-a. The growing upper
 400| eigenvalue 1+(q-1)a causes no problem: no bounded global upper spectrum is
 401| assumed by (C1), and energy is exactly (n-1)theta^2.
 402| 
 403| **Hypotheses other than W.** T1-F: H0 holds with A=1, phi0^2=c,
 404| M=theta^2+1 and g0=1, since global floor c gives both SE conditions for all
 405| sizes and fixed theta gives BM-infinity. This also proves FL-16 and FL-Q.
 406| For every |U|<=15 excluding the truth, Var_G(1|U)>=c and
 407| 
 408|     delta_{U,1}^2=theta^2(n-1)Var_G(1|U)>=theta^2(n-1)c;
 409| 
 410| so V holds with M_n=theta^2(n-1)c/log n. All outside-Q columns are orthogonal
 411| to the group and one another, so L-gain holds uniformly with eta=0.
 412| L-size^b holds by the floor definition; K=p>=2q+33 eventually, proving
 413| L-feas. BM-Q, and hence BM-W, follows from
 414|  theta^2 nc/[sigma^2(q+log n)]->infinity. No coefficient magnitude restriction
 415| beyond fixed theta!=0 is needed.
 416| 
 417| **Direct width bound.** Write g_i=e_i'g, independent standard normals. For
 418| l<=q outside a lattice T, put t=|T|>=1. The regression coefficients on T
 419| are all A_t=a/(1-a+ta), so 0<=t A_t<=1. Its unnormalised residual is
 420| 
 421|     sqrt(a)(1-t A_t)e_0
 422|        +sqrt(1-a)(e_l-A_t sum_{j in T}e_j).
 423| 
 424| Its squared norm is v_t=(1-a)[1+a/(1-a+ta)]>=1-a. Division by sqrt(v_t)
 425| therefore yields, simultaneously for all these pairs,
 426| 
 427|     |u_{T,l}'g| <= 2 max_{j<=q}|g_j| + sqrt(a/(1-a)) |g_0|.  (5.1)
 428| 
 429| Let U be the maximum of the left side for within-group pairs, and V the
 430| maximum for outside-Q pairs. Outside directions are exactly e_l, hence
 431| 
 432|     E U <= 2 sqrt(2 log(2q)) + sqrt(a/(1-a)) sqrt(2/pi),
 433|     E V <= sqrt(2 log(2(p-q))).
 434| 
 435| For all sufficiently large n both families are nonempty. Each of U,V is
 436| 1-Lipschitz as a maximum of absolute unit Gaussian projections. The Gaussian
 437| upper-tail bound and integration give
 438| 
 439|     E max(U,V) <= max(EU,EV) + C_G,
 440|     C_G = integral_0^infinity min(1,2 exp(-t^2/2)) dt < infinity.
 441| 
 442| This last constant follows by the union bound on U-EU and V-EV; independence
 443| of U and V is not required. Consequently
 444| 
 445|     E max_P |u_{T,l}'g|
 446|        <= max(sqrt(8b log n)+O_a(1), sqrt(2 log n)+O(1)).       (5.2)
 447| 
 448| Choose a fixed delta>0 so small that
 449| 
 450|     2delta < min(1-2b, 3-10b).
 451| 
 452| Since log p=log n-log 3+o(1), (5.2) is strictly below
 453| sqrt(2 log p+(1-2b-2delta)log n) eventually, with a positive multiple of
 454| sqrt(log n) to spare. This is exactly (W-unif) with
 455| 0<delta<(1-2b)/2; thus W follows by RM2 `lemmas/L2_width.md:123-140`.
 456| Equivalently the width gap is bounded above by [SW1-7]
 457| 
 458|     [max(sqrt(8b),sqrt(2))-sqrt(3-2b)] sqrt(log n)+O_a(1),
 459| 
 460| which tends to minus infinity for b<3/10. The size-dependent level has been
 461| minimised at k=q (outside-group pairs allow T=Q, since q<K); its squared value is
 462| log(n+1)+2log(p/(q+1))=(3-2b)log n+O(1).
 463| 
 464| This verifies every C1 hypothesis on a nonempty range of fixed positive
 465| correlations. It does not verify the heuristic 8b<2A+1 range: that comparison
 466| omits the -2b contribution from the model-size penalty. For b>=3/10 this
 467| particular upper bound ceases to prove W; that is neither a converse nor
 468| an assertion that another sufficient form or a sharper computation fails.
 469| [LC2C-1] The range is not claimed sharp. The check LC2-C observes that (5.1) is
 470| nearly attained only at small |T|, where the level is about sqrt(3 log n), and
 471| sketches (W) for b<3/8 by a size-by-size comparison, with a matching sketch
 472| that the width gap is positive for b>3/8. Neither is proved here; recorded in
 473| RM2 `SHARPNESS.md` §4 (open item O4').
 474|

You are an independent expert referee assessing the SHARPNESS of mathematical results in a research project on the
asymptotic theory of a sequential Monte Carlo method for Bayesian variable selection (linear regression, p <= n^A, often
p >> n). Every result is asymptotic; finite-n behaviour is not a defect. The project's main risk is publishing theorems
that are correct but weaker than what is achievable.

You receive the working files of one ticket and a list of headline claims located by file and line span. Ignore any
status, score or review verdict the files assert. Take each claim as correct; your job is NOT to re-check the proof.

For each claim assess:
(a) hypotheses: is any assumption stronger than the proof needs (say which weaker condition suffices, with the step
    where it is used), or is it necessary (give a counterexample or a known lower bound showing that)?
(b) conclusion: is the rate, constant regime, scaling range (e.g. the exponent range for p vs n, beta-min level, sparsity
    growth) or mode of convergence improvable? Compare with the best known results for Bayesian variable selection
    (e.g. Johnson-Rossell, Narisetty-He, Castillo-Schmidt-Hieber-van der Vaart, Yang-Wainwright-Jordan MCMC mixing,
    Song-Liang, Zhou-Yang-Chang-Liang); cite only results you are confident about, and say when you are unsure.
(c) the cheapest concrete route to a stronger version, if one exists, and how hard it looks.

Severity: SHARP = no improvement you can justify; IMPROVABLE-EASY = a stronger version follows with a modest change you
can describe; IMPROVABLE-HARD = a stronger version is plausible or known elsewhere but needs new work; UNCLEAR = cannot
judge from the material.

Output, in this order:
1. For each claim, a short section: claim id, the assessment (a)-(c) with exact locations (file:line).
2. Then exactly one line per claim, nothing after the last one:
SHARP <claim id> VERDICT=<SHARP|IMPROVABLE-EASY|IMPROVABLE-HARD|UNCLEAR>

  12| 1, so it is its own standardisation: X = X^r, D_x = I, θ* = β. σ² > 0 fixed; p = p_n with p ≤ n^A.

  15| ## L11.1 Example F-1: orthogonal design (F1 with η = 0; F2)
  16|

  18| sufficiently large n.

   1| # L1 — Lemma AGG (table identities) and FLOOR — claims (C0), (T0)
   2| 
   3| Status: **PROVED (by this seat)**. The check record is kept outside this file (the ticket's final checkpoint file and `reviews/`). Deterministic: no probability is used anywhere in this file.
   4| Statement proved: `STATEMENT.md` §5.1 (C0) (AGG-a)–(AGG-d), (FLOOR), and §5.3 (T0). Notation of `STATEMENT.md` §1–§2.
   5| 
   6| ## L1.0 Setting, conventions, elementary facts
   7| 
   8| Valid inputs, n ≥ 4, EX-A. {C_b} is any partition of [p] with |C_b| ≤ min(16, K). S₀ ∈ Ω is **any** reference model,
   9| s₀ := |S₀|, U*_b := S₀ ∩ C_b, 𝔹* := {b : U*_b ≠ ∅}; Q ⊇ S₀ with |Q| ≤ K; c_Q := |Q| + 15s₀.
  10| Tables: r_b(U) := m(U)/m(∅) for U ⊆ C_b; r_b(U) ∈ (0, ∞) by (L1.5)(i) below. γ₀(S) := w(|S|)∏_b r_b(S ∩ C_b) for
  11| S ∈ Ω = {|S| ≤ K}; π₀ = γ₀/Σ_Ω γ₀. w(k) := ½/C(2p − 1, k) is used as a formula for every integer 0 ≤ k ≤ 2p − 1.
  12| Parts L1.1–L1.4 use **only**: r_b > 0, the formula for w, K ≤ p, and the block-size bound. Rising factorial:
  13| (x)_a := x(x + 1)⋯(x + a − 1), (x)_0 := 1.
  14| 
  15| **(P1)** w(k + 1)/w(k) = (k + 1)/(2p − 1 − k) for 0 ≤ k ≤ 2p − 2; it is ≤ (k + 1)/p when k ≤ p − 1.
  16| **(P2)** w(k − 1)/w(k) = (2p − k)/k for 1 ≤ k ≤ 2p − 1; it is ≤ 2p, and it is ≥ p/k when k ≤ p.
  17| *Proof.* C(2p − 1, k + 1)/C(2p − 1, k) = (2p − 1 − k)/(k + 1). ∎
  18| 
  19| **(P3) Path bound.** For integers 0 ≤ D ≤ k ≤ p and a ≥ 0 with k − D + a ≤ p:
  20|   w(k − D + a)/w(k) ≤ (2p)^D · p^{−a} · (k − D + 1)_a.
  21| *Proof.* w(k − D)/w(k) = ∏_{i=0}^{D−1} w(k − i − 1)/w(k − i) ≤ (2p)^D by (P2) (k − i ≥ 1). And
  22| w(k − D + a)/w(k − D) = ∏_{i=0}^{a−1}(k − D + i + 1)/(2p − 1 − (k − D + i)) ≤ ∏_{i=0}^{a−1}(k − D + i + 1)/p by (P1), because
  23| k − D + i ≤ k − D + a − 1 ≤ p − 1. ∎
  24| 
  25| **(P4)** For 0 ≤ u < 1 and real c > 0: Σ_{a≥0}(c)_a u^a/a! = (1 − u)^{−c} (binomial series).
  26| **(P5)** For a finite set L and m_l ≥ 0: Σ_{N⊆L, |N|=a}∏_{l∈N}m_l ≤ (Σ_{l∈L}m_l)^a/a!.
  27| *Proof.* (Σ_l m_l)^a is the sum of ∏ m_{l_i} over ordered a-tuples; each a-subset contributes a! tuples. ∎
  28| 
  29| **(CH) Chain bound.** Recall m_l := max{r_b(T ∪ {l})/r_b(T) : U*_b ⊆ T ⊆ C_b ∖ {l}}, b = b(l), for l ∉ S₀. Let T ⊆ C_b with
  30| U*_b ⊆ T and N ⊆ C_b ∖ T with N ∩ S₀ = ∅. Then r_b(T ∪ N)/r_b(T) ≤ ∏_{l∈N}m_l.
  31| *Proof.* Enumerate N = {l₁, …, l_a} and put T_i := T ∪ {l₁, …, l_i}. Then r_b(T ∪ N)/r_b(T) = ∏_{i=1}^a r_b(T_{i−1} ∪ {l_i})/r_b(T_{i−1}),
  32| and U*_b ⊆ T_{i−1} ⊆ C_b ∖ {l_i}, so each factor is ≤ m_{l_i}. ∎
  33| 
  34| ## L1.1 Decomposition of a model relative to the lattice
  35| 
  36| For S ∈ Ω put U_b := S ∩ C_b and **T(S) := (S ∩ Q) ∪ S₀**. Then S₀ ⊆ T(S) ⊆ Q, so T(S) ∈ 𝓛(Q) ⊆ Ω (|T(S)| ≤ |Q| ≤ K), and
  37| S ∈ 𝓛(Q) ⟺ S = T(S). Write T_b := T(S) ∩ C_b = (U_b ∩ Q) ∪ U*_b.
  38| * Block b is **bad for S** if U*_b ⊄ U_b (then b ∈ 𝔹*); put d_b := |U*_b ∖ U_b| ≥ 1 and a_b := |U_b ∖ Q|. Then
  39|   T_b = T_b(U_b) in the notation of `STATEMENT.md` §2, |U_b| = |T_b| − d_b + a_b, and a_b ≤ 15 (U_b ∖ Q ⊆ C_b ∖ U*_b and
  40|   U*_b ≠ ∅).
  41| * Otherwise b is **good for S**: U_b = T_b ⊔ N_b with T_b = U_b ∩ Q ⊇ U*_b and N_b := U_b ∖ Q.
  42| S is determined by T(S), its set of bad blocks, the sets U_b of the bad blocks, and N := ⊔_{b good}N_b ⊆ [p] ∖ Q.
  43| 
  44| **Lemma L1.1 (fibre bound).** For every T ∈ 𝓛(Q), every sub-family 𝔹′ ⊆ 𝔹* and every a′ ≥ 0, let 𝒮(T, 𝔹′, a′) be the set
  45| of S ∈ Ω with T(S) = T, set of bad blocks 𝔹′, and |N| = a′. Then
  46|   Σ_{S∈𝒮(T,𝔹′,a′)} γ₀(S) ≤ γ₀(T)·∏_{b∈𝔹′}Ξ_b(Q)·(κ₀ + 1)_{a′}·U_Q^{a′}/a′!,   κ₀ := c_Q if 𝔹′ ≠ ∅, κ₀ := |T| if 𝔹′ = ∅.
  47| 
  48| *Proof.* Fix S ∈ 𝒮(T, 𝔹′, a′). Put D := Σ_{b∈𝔹′}(d_b − a_b)₊ and E := Σ_{b∈𝔹′}(a_b − d_b)₊. Then |S| = |T| − D + E + a′,
  49| D ≤ Σ_{b∈𝔹′}d_b ≤ s₀ ≤ |T|, and |S| ≤ K ≤ p. By (P3) with k := |T| and a := E + a′,
  50|   w(|S|)/w(|T|) ≤ (2p)^D p^{−E−a′}(x)_{E+a′},   x := |T| − D + 1,   (x)_{E+a′} = (x)_E·(x + E)_{a′}.
  51| If 𝔹′ = ∅ then D = E = 0 and (x)_{a′} = (|T| + 1)_{a′}. If 𝔹′ ≠ ∅: E ≤ Σ_{b∈𝔹′}a_b ≤ 15s₀ and |T| ≤ |Q|, so
  52| x + E − 1 ≤ |T| + E ≤ c_Q; hence (x)_E ≤ (x + E − 1)^E ≤ c_Q^E (also when E = 0) and (x + E)_{a′} ≤ (c_Q + 1)_{a′}. In both cases

 101|   (I − P_{U₀})CW_l = m + ẽ,   m := ΠW_{S₀∖U₀}γ²,   ẽ := Πe.

 104| and e keeps its law N(0, τ_e²I_n). If μ̃ ≠ 0 put v := μ̃/‖μ̃‖ ∈ 𝒱 and
 105|   ξ := ⟨ẽ, v⟩/τ_e,   d₀ := ⟨m, v⟩/τ_e,   R := ‖(Π − vvᵀ)(m + ẽ)‖²/τ_e².

 107| components); |d₀| ≤ d̄ := m̄/√c_Σ on CN. Since x̃_l = (m + ẽ)/t_l, ρ̂_{U₀,l} = ⟨m + ẽ, v⟩/‖m + ẽ‖ and
 108|   **g²_{U₀,l} = N·(ξ + d₀)²/((ξ + d₀)² + R).**                                                            (9.1)
 109| (If μ̃ = 0 then δ_{U₀,l} = 0, a_{U₀} = 1 and the term is F(0, 1) = √(2/π)z_n; put g_{U₀,l} := 0.)

 111| A noncentral χ² dominates the central one stochastically, ν₀ − 1 ≥ N − 16, and P(χ²_k < k − 2√(kx)) ≤ e^{−x}; so
 112| P(E_R(l, U₀)ᶜ | 𝒲) ≤ n^{−(A+2)} and P(E_ξ(l, U₀)ᶜ | 𝒲) ≤ 2n^{−(A+2)}. On E_R: g² ≤ κ_n²(ξ + d₀)², κ_n := (1 − η_n)^{−1/2}.
 113| 
 114| **Lemma L9.5.** For n large (η_n ≤ a̲/2), for every l ∉ Q and U₀ ∈ I_l:
 115|   E[F(g_{U₀,l}, a_{U₀})·1_{E_R(l,U₀)}·1_{CN}] ≤ **Φ_n := √(2/a̲)·√(2/π)·z̄_n·exp(η_nz̄_n²/a̲ + 2d̄z̄_n/a̲ + d̄²/a̲)**.

 117| (9.1), F(g_{U₀,l}, a)1_{E_R} ≤ F(κ_n(ξ + d₀), a), and ξ ~ N(0, 1) given 𝒲. With s′ := κ_n√(1 − a), r := √a:
 118| s′² = (1 − a)/(1 − η_n) < 1 and 1 − s′² = (a − η_n)/(1 − η_n) ≥ a̲/2. For fixed Z, with c := s′d₀ + rZ:
 119| E_ξ exp((s′ξ + c)²/2) = (1 − s′²)^{−1/2}exp(c²/(2(1 − s′²))). Therefore
 120|   E_ξF(κ_n(ξ + d₀), a) = (1 − s′²)^{−1/2}∫_{−z_n}^{z_n}exp((s′d₀ + rZ)²/(2(1 − s′²)) − Z²/2)dZ/√(2π).
 121| The exponent equals ½Z²[r²/(1 − s′²) − 1] + s′rd₀Z/(1 − s′²) + s′²d₀²/(2(1 − s′²)), and r²/(1 − s′²) − 1 = η_n(1 − a)/(a − η_n) ≤ 2η_n/a̲,
 122| s′r/(1 − s′²) ≤ 2/a̲, s′²/(2(1 − s′²)) ≤ 1/a̲. On |Z| ≤ z_n ≤ z̄_n the exponent is ≤ η_nz̄_n²/a̲ + 2d̄z̄_n/a̲ + d̄²/a̲; ∫_{−z_n}^{z_n}dZ/√(2π) = √(2/π)z_n ≤ √(2/π)z̄_n; and
 123| (1 − s′²)^{−1/2} ≤ √(2/a̲). Take expectations over 𝒲. ∎

 126| innovation e is independent of W_D. No law is asserted given E_cov or given a sample covariance.

 130| **E := E_cov ∩ ⋂{E_R(l, U₀) ∩ E_ξ(l, U₀) : l ∉ Q, U₀ ∈ I_l}.** P(Eᶜ) ≤ 4n^{−2} + p·N_ref·3n^{−(A+2)} ≤ (4 + 3N_ref)n^{−2} → 0.

 135| (G_n + z̄_n = O(√log n), ι_n√log n → 0, ε_n² log n → 0). With L9.3, for every l ∉ Q, on E:
 136|   max{J_n(δ_{U,l}, τ_U) : U ∌ l, |U| ≤ 15} ≤ √(2/π)z̄_n + e^{ς′_n}Σ_{U₀∈I_l}F(g_{U₀,l}, a_{U₀})1_{E_R(l,U₀)}1_{CN}

 138|   on E:  **𝔏_n(Q) ≤ √(2/π)z̄_n + e^{ς′_n}Ψ_n**,   Ψ_n := p⁻¹Σ_{l∉Q}Σ_{U₀∈I_l}F(g_{U₀,l}, a_{U₀})1_{E_R(l,U₀)}1_{CN},   **E Ψ_n ≤ N_refΦ_n** (L9.5).

 140|   **P(𝔏_n(Q) > √(2/π)z̄_n + e·λ·N_ref·Φ_n) ≤ P(Eᶜ) + 1/λ.**                                              (9.2)

 142| N_ref = exp(O(log log n)). Taking λ = log n in (9.2): with probability → 1,
 143|   **𝔏_n(Q) ≤ exp(C_B√log n),   C_B := 2d̄√(2A + 1)/a̲ + 1**   (n large).

 147| tightness. No concentration argument across columns is supplied; a fixed-constant bound with probability tending to

params.system:
You are an independent expert referee assessing the SHARPNESS of mathematical results in a research project on the
asymptotic theory of a sequential Monte Carlo method for Bayesian variable selection (linear regression, p <= n^A, often
p >> n). Every result is asymptotic; finite-n behaviour is not a defect. The project's main risk is publishing theorems
that are correct but weaker than what is achievable.

You receive the working files of one ticket and a list of headline claims located by file and line span. Ignore any
status, score or review verdict the files assert. Take each claim as correct; your job is NOT to re-check the proof.

For each claim assess:
(a) hypotheses: is any assumption stronger than the proof needs (say which weaker condition suffices, with the step
    where it is used), or is it necessary (give a counterexample or a known lower bound showing that)?
(b) conclusion: is the rate, constant regime, scaling range (e.g. the exponent range for p vs n, beta-min level, sparsity
    growth) or mode of convergence improvable? Compare with the best known results for Bayesian variable selection
    (e.g. Johnson-Rossell, Narisetty-He, Castillo-Schmidt-Hieber-van der Vaart, Yang-Wainwright-Jordan MCMC mixing,
    Song-Liang, Zhou-Yang-Chang-Liang); cite only results you are confident about, and say when you are unsure.
(c) the cheapest concrete route to a stronger version, if one exists, and how hard it looks.

Severity: SHARP = no improvement you can justify; IMPROVABLE-EASY = a stronger version follows with a modest change you
can describe; IMPROVABLE-HARD = a stronger version is plausible or known elsewhere but needs new work; UNCLEAR = cannot
judge from the material.

Output, in this order:
1. For each claim, a short section: claim id, the assessment (a)-(c) with exact locations (file:line).
2. Then exactly one line per claim, nothing after the last one:
SHARP <claim id> VERDICT=<SHARP|IMPROVABLE-EASY|IMPROVABLE-HARD|UNCLEAR>

  17| contains j; the blocks are disjoint, so C_{b(l)} = C for every l ∈ I. Then S₀ ∪ I ⊆ C. This union is disjoint and has
  18| s₀ + (17 − s₀) = 17 elements, but |C| ≤ 16: a contradiction. ∎

  27| * If s₀ ≥ 16: I_n = {l_n}. The set U*_{b(l_n)} = S₀ ∩ C_{b(l_n)} lies in C_{b(l_n)} ∖ {l_n}, so it has at most 15 < s₀ elements:
  28|   it is a proper subset of S₀.
  29| * If 1 ≤ s₀ ≤ 15: |I_n| = 17 − s₀, and by Lemma P3.1 the set {l ∈ I_n : U*_{b(l)} ⊊ S₀} is not empty; let l_n be its
  30|   smallest element. Here |U*_{b(l_n)}| ≤ s₀ − 1 ≤ 14.
  31| 
  32| In both cases l_n is a null column determined by X and I_n (no use of the response), and V := U*_{b(l_n)} is a proper
  33| subset of S₀ with |V| ≤ 15. By hypothesis, δ²_{V,l_n} ≥ c·τ²_V·log n at V = U*_{b(l_n)}. This is the premise of (C2)(i) on the
  34| actual partition with the null l_n and the same constant c > 1 + 2Ā; (C2)(i) gives the claim. ((C2) is stated under
  35| [TK]; under (E) and (GF-16), [TK] holds by (B-TK), BASE `STATEMENT.md:233`; the proof in BASE `lemmas/L7_NEC.md:14-26`

  40| (BASE `STATEMENT.md:320-321`), so (N2) asserts nothing there. Hence (T4⁺) implies (T4).

  42| ## P3.3 The premise of (N2⁺) can hold (1 ≤ s₀ ≤ 15)

  44| **Example P3.3** (an example, not a hypothesis of any claim). Fix s := s₀ ∈ {1, …, 15}, r := 17 − s, θ ≠ 0, σ² > 0 and
  45| c > 1. Let p := 17, S₀ := {1, …, s}, I := {s + 1, …, 17}, and for n ≥ 18
  46|   ρ_n² := c·(σ² + sθ²)·log n/((n − 1)θ²)  (ρ_n > 0),   G_n := [[I_s, ρ_n·1_s1_rᵀ], [ρ_n·1_r1_sᵀ, I_r]] ∈ ℝ^{17×17}.
  47| * *G_n is positive definite for large n.* G_n = I + ρ_nB with B := [[0, 1_s1_rᵀ], [1_r1_sᵀ, 0]]; B has rank 2 and its non-zero
  48|   eigenvalues are ±√(sr) (B² = diag(r·1_s1_sᵀ, s·1_r1_rᵀ), with largest eigenvalue sr). So the eigenvalues of G_n are
  49|   1 − ρ_n√(sr), 1, 1 + ρ_n√(sr). Since sr ≤ 72 and ρ_n → 0: λ_min(G_n) ≥ ½ for large n.
  50| * *The design.* Let O be n × 17 with orthonormal columns orthogonal to 1_n (n ≥ 18), and X := √(n − 1)·O·G_n^{1/2}. The
  51|   columns of X are centred and XᵀX = (n − 1)G_n, so each column has sample variance 1: X is a standardised design
